questions.q: How many comparisons does linear search make to find 17 in the list [8, -4, 7, 17, 0, 2, 19]? Use the method 'Comparisons Made by Linear Search'. Work with: size = 1024, zero_index = 5. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of unchecked.
questions.a: 1018 units

questions.q: Determine the position of 8, 1, 99 and 44 in the list [1, -2, 32, 8, 17, 19, 42, 13, 0, 44] by linear search and note the comparisons each takes.. Use the method 'Comparisons Made by Linear Search'. Work with: size = 1024, zero_index = 100. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of unchecked.
questions.a: 923 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Comparisons Made by Linear Search' refers to.
questions.a: Linear search compares the key with each element from the first onwards and stops at the first match; the key sitting at zero-based index i costs i plus one comparisons, and the rest of the list stays unchecked.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Comparisons Made by Linear Search'.
questions.a: Finding 17 in [8, -4, 7, 17, 0, 2, 19] takes 4 comparisons because three elements precede it.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Comparisons Made by Linear Search', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: unchecked = size - (zero_index + 1)

concepts.title: Best and Worst Work of Linear Search

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Best and Worst Work of Linear Search' refers to.
questions.a: The workload of linear search swings with the key's location: a key at the front needs a single comparison, while a key at the last position, or one that is absent, forces comparisons with all n elements.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Best and Worst Work of Linear Search'.
questions.a: Searching for 43 in an 11-element list that ends with 43 costs the full 11 comparisons.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Best and Worst Work of Linear Search', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: best = 1 comparison; worst = n comparisons

questions.q: Using the method 'Middle Position in Binary Search', work with: first = 400, last = 80. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mid.
questions.a: 240 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Middle Position in Binary Search' and work with: first = 3, last = 20. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of mid.
questions.a: 11 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Middle Position in Binary Search' refers to.
questions.a: Binary search keeps two markers, first and last, on a sorted list and probes the midpoint computed by floor-dividing their sum by two, so for ten elements the probe lands on index 5, the sixth element.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Middle Position in Binary Search'.
questions.a: When the middle element equals the key the search ends immediately, as 17 found at index 7 shows.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Middle Position in Binary Search', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: mid = (first + last) // 2

questions.q: Using the method 'Halving the Search Area', work with: size = 512. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of after_three.
questions.a: 64 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Halving the Search Area' and work with: size = 2048. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of after_three.
questions.a: 256 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Halving the Search Area' refers to.
questions.a: After every unsuccessful midpoint comparison, binary search discards half the remaining list, so a 15-element search area shrinks to 7, then 3, then 1 element across successive iterations.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Halving the Search Area'.
questions.a: Searching key 2 in the 15-element list takes four iterations because 15 halves to 7, 3 and finally 1.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Halving the Search Area', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: remaining = previous // 2

questions.q: Using the method 'Linear versus Binary Workload', work with: exponent = 3. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of half.
questions.a: 4 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Linear versus Binary Workload' and work with: exponent = 8. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of half.
questions.a: 128 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Linear versus Binary Workload' refers to.
questions.a: Locating a record at the exact middle of a sorted database costs one comparison for binary search but about half the database for linear search, which is why ordered data rewards binary searching enormously.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Linear versus Binary Workload'.
questions.a: For 2 to the power 30 records, a middle-position hit costs one comparison in binary search but 536870912 in linear search.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Linear versus Binary Workload', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: half = 2 ** exponent / 2

questions.q: Using the method 'Hash Value by Remainder Method', work with: element = 10, table_size = 512. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of position.
questions.a: 11 units

questions.q: Take the relation taught for 'Hash Value by Remainder Method' and work with: element = 6, table_size = 4096. Carry the chain through step by step and give the final value of position.
questions.a: 7 units

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Hash Value by Remainder Method' refers to.
questions.a: Hashing computes an element's home slot directly: the remainder method divides the element by the hash table size and uses the remainder as the index, so checking presence needs just one comparison regardless of list size.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Hash Value by Remainder Method'.
questions.a: In the table of size 10, element 16 lands in slot 6 and is reported at position 7.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Hash Value by Remainder Method', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: position = element % table_size + 1

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Collision and Perfect Hash Functions' refers to.
questions.a: A collision happens when two elements share one hash slot, as 16 and 26 both mapping to 6 under a modulo-10 function; a hash function that gives every element a unique slot is called perfect, and collision resolution decides where the extras go.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Collision and Perfect Hash Functions'.
questions.a: With a perfect hash function, collisions never arise and every search stays a single comparison.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Collision and Perfect Hash Functions', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: h(16) = 6 and h(26) = 6 -> collision

concepts.title: Sorted List Requirement for Binary Search

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Sorted List Requirement for Binary Search' refers to.
questions.a: Binary search only works when the list is already ordered, because each midpoint comparison decides which half can still hold the key; on unsorted data it would discard the wrong half, so the data must be sorted first.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sorted List Requirement for Binary Search'.
questions.a: A dictionary search for Zoology starts in the second half only because the words are alphabetically arranged.

questions.q: Write the standard relation used for 'Sorted List Requirement for Binary Search', in plain ASCII form.
questions.a: sorted list + mid comparison -> discard one half
